messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

That gray morning in Portland harbor, three years ago, changed everything for Ingrid. She was preparing her fishing trawler for departure when police officers boarded, responding to a mistaken smuggling report. Within minutes, the encounter turned violent: an officer shoved her against the wheelhouse bulkhead, another struck her shoulder with a baton as she tried to explain she was the captain. She was handcuffed and held on the dock for four hours before being released without charges. The physical bruises faded, but the memory of that morning became seared into her mind with photographic clarity—every detail, the officer's face inches from hers, the cold metal, the crushing helplessness, as clear as if captured on film.

Now seventy-six, widowed for over a decade, Ingrid still captains the same trawler, but the work has taken on a desperate quality. Whenever a quiet moment threatens—a lull between hauls, the minutes waiting for the tide—the memories surge back, and she relives the event as though it is happening again: her heart pounds, her breath shortens, and she feels the same visceral fear. To escape this, she throws herself into overwork. She takes double shifts, repairs nets that don't need mending, scrubs the deck until her hands ache—anything to keep her mind occupied. There is no space in her day for idle thought; she has learned that stillness invites the reliving, so she stays in motion.

Yet the overworking itself feeds the memories. Exhaustion lowers her defenses, and after fourteen-hour days, when she finally lies down in her small cabin, the reliving is most vivid. She also cannot stop replaying why the event happened to her—she goes over and over the officers' motives, her own actions, the random chance that put her in that harbor at that moment. This rumination on meaning holds no answers, but she is trapped in it, and each cycle makes the memory feel more solid, more photographically exact. And she dwells on how she used to be before the assault: the confident, unquestioned captain who moved through her vessel with ease. That woman feels like a stranger now, and the more she compares her present self to her past self, the clearer the traumatic image becomes, as though the past is the only reality that remains vivid.

Her overworking has strained her relationship with her first mate, who has begun to worry openly about her health. Last month, when he suggested she take a day off, she snapped at him—not because she disagreed, but because she was terrified that any pause would let the memories flood in unchecked. She now avoids even short rests, and her social world has narrowed to the repetitive tasks of the trawler. The consequence is concrete: she is more isolated, more brittle, and the first mate has started to avoid her when he can.

What finally brought Ingrid to seek help was her seventy-sixth birthday, which she spent alone on the boat, working. She realized she could not remember the last time she felt at peace—only the relentless cycle: memory driving her into work, work feeding the memory. She is afraid that if she slows down, she will be trapped in reliving, unable to function. But she is also desperate to break the loop, to find a way to let the memory fade without having to exhaust herself to keep it at bay.
